course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 5
unit.description: Follow Manifest Destiny and the Mexican–American War, the sectional conflict over slavery, the election of 1860 and secession, the Civil War, and Reconstruction and its failure from 1844 to 1877.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Contextualizing Period 5
lesson.summary: A map of Period 5 (1844–1877): expansion and migration, debates over rights and citizenship, and the sectional conflict that led to the Civil War and Reconstruction.
learningGoals: Explain the context in which sectional conflict emerged from 1844 to 1877.
Describe how expansion and migration connected the United States to the wider world.
Trace how debates over slavery led to civil war and to the contested reconstruction of the South.
lesson.bigIdea: Expansion, migration, and debates over slavery pushed the nation toward civil war, and the Union's victory ended slavery and secession but left the meaning of citizenship contested.
lesson.context: Contextualization, the CED skill for this topic, means placing an event or a source in the broader setting of its time. For Period 5 the setting is a nation that was growing quickly in territory and population while it divided over slavery.

sections.title: Expansion and new connections

blocks.text: Between 1844 and 1877, the United States became more connected with the world, pursued an expansionist foreign policy in the Western Hemisphere, and emerged as the destination for many migrants from other countries. Popular enthusiasm for expansion, supported by economic and security interests, led to the acquisition of new territories, to substantial migration westward, and to new overseas initiatives.

By 1848 the nation reached the Pacific Ocean through the annexation of Texas, an agreement with Britain over the Oregon country, and the lands taken from Mexico. Migration from Europe, mainly from Ireland and Germany, increased the population of the Northern states, and trade with Asia grew.

sections.takeaway: By 1848 the United States reached from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and its population was growing through migration.

sections.title: Debates over rights and citizenship

blocks.text: In the 1840s and 1850s, Americans continued to debate questions about rights and citizenship for various groups of U.S. inhabitants. The groups included enslaved and free African Americans, women, immigrants, American Indians, and the Mexicans who lived in the lands that the United States acquired. These debates built on earlier arguments about the Declaration of Independence's claim that “all men are created equal.”

After the Civil War, the same questions returned in new forms. Reconstruction and the Civil War ended slavery, altered the relationship between the states and the federal government, and led to debates over new definitions of citizenship, particularly regarding the rights of African Americans, women, and other minorities.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Period 5 was not only about slavery. Slavery divided the nation most deeply, but questions about immigrants, women, and American Indians ran alongside it.

sections.takeaway: Debates over who belonged and who held rights began before the war and continued after it.

sections.title: From sectional conflict to Reconstruction

blocks.text: Intensified by expansion and deepening regional divisions, debates over slavery and other economic, cultural, and political issues led the nation into civil war. Debates over slavery came to dominate political discussion in the 1850s, and they culminated in the bitter election of 1860 and the secession of Southern states.

The North's greater manpower and industrial resources, the leadership of Abraham Lincoln and others, and the decision to emancipate enslaved people eventually led to the Union's military victory in the devastating Civil War. The Union victory and the contested reconstruction of the South settled the issues of slavery and secession, but they left unresolved many questions about the power of the federal government and the rights of citizens.

Keep the order of events in mind: the Mexican–American War (1846–1848), the Compromise of 1850, the Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854), the Dred Scott decision (1857), Lincoln's election (1860), the Civil War (1861–1865), and Reconstruction (1865–1877).

sections.takeaway: A war over expansion opened a period of sectional conflict, a civil war ended slavery, and Reconstruction left the rights of citizens unsettled.

connections.title: Where the story begins
connections.body: The disputes of Period 5 grew out of the westward spread of slavery in Period 4. Topic 5.2 follows the drive to expand to the Pacific.
connections.transferQuestion: Which development from Period 4 do you think did the most to prepare the sectional conflict that followed?
connections.feedback: A strong answer picks one development, such as the westward movement of slavery or the Missouri Compromise, and connects it to the conflicts over slavery in new territories after 1844.
